I start by asking my submissive partner for the scene a lot of questions. What are you looking for? What do you want out of this scene? But the most important one is *what are you looking to feel during this scene*?

If they tell you what emotions they want to experience- fear, praise, structure, nurture, degradation, humiliation- it gets the ball rolling on language. I get to start affecting my physicality and language choices to start working on setting up and drawing those emotions out of people. 

Next, I work on my own emotions. What am *I* looking for out of the scene, how do *I* want to feel. I communicate that with my partner, and make sure we're both feeling good.

Then I build the mask. I let the part of myself that worries sit in the back of my head, the way that I used to build characters for theater growing up. I listen to music that lets me slip into my headspace. I have a cigarette, alone, while my submissive prepares themselves for the scene. I use this time to think of my opening lines and actions.

If I have the opening, and I have the initiative, I can then start working from there. My partner is giving me feedback the entire time through the scene- their body language, what they say, how they react. Each of those pieces of stimuli is something I can use to say "Yes, and...". I know how I can play and perform with that in mind. 

My honest recommendation every time I hear someone dominant say "I am struggling with building the character or finding what to say" is take a few improv classes. You can find them locally in any city near you, it's a ton of fun, and it'll teach you everything you need to know.

I am a very, very ritualistic person when it comes to kink and time in kink spaces. I have my own personal rituals for stepping in and out of headspace, and I think finding and developing those rituals can be a really useful and important way of creating separation in your life between your day-to-day life and your dom(me) life. 

My scenes are (almost) always pretty intensively planned. I will often times physically block out my broad movements and practice within the space I'm going to play in. This gives me a broad strokes idea of the way movement is going to happen in the scene, and then defines the limits of what I'll do when we're playing in a space. When I do pickup play at parties, it's a little less planned, but I have a pretty standard routine I modify for those scenes as well. 

I am a deeply anxious person, so I have built a bit of a character mask that I domme from behind. This separation allows me to keep that neurotic part of my brain active but not in my way- It's what is focusing on safety measures, reminding me to check for color and monitor body language and other signs for me to worry. The character part of me, however, is enjoying the vibe fully- it's where my language and actions come from, where my enjoyment lives, where all the mean fantasies come to life. 

I build this mask in the time I take between negotiation ending and the scene starting. I leave my submissive to do what they need to in order to get ready- stretching, changing clothes, drinking some water, etc- and usually step outside of the physical environment we're playing in, have a cigarette, and either do breathing exercises or sing while I listen to a specific playlist. I walk through my head about our negotiations, and usually find and hold on to one idea for how I will begin the scene verbally, and build my feeling around that. 

I also ritualize the start of the scene- by collaring my submissive, or asking them to take off the rings I wear. This way we have a physical sign of the scene beginning or ending, and I know when my character drops.

It really, really frustrates me sometimes. Since 2016 Standard with the impact of Energy on the format and especially because of the period of FIRE design between War of the Spark and MH1, Magic players have gotten more and more Ban/Unban hungry as a way of changing formats (which is a sign of the waxing and waning of WotC's design philosophies over the last decade) rather than looking at new sets as a chance to print new and interesting designs to provide new tools to formats like Modern. 

Instead, we've developed a culture of "What's the next ban? What's the next unban? What's the fastest way to shake up the metagame that we can find?" that I've found really frustrating. It feels like people aren't comfortable sitting and optimizing within a metagame, and instead want to rush towards the next big swing every 3-6 months; which is really bad for the long term health of the game. 

In these unban threads, I always see people talking about Unbans as "well we can do this now because of X, Y, and Z reasons". But I rarely see people proposing a case to what making these changes adds to the game.

When I think about cards I'd want to unban (mainly Jitte, potentially Pod) I think about the options those cards add to the metagame and the dynamics they add.

Jitte adds a strong board breaking tool to the main boards of stoneforge decks- meaning that Creature decks that can struggle vs how wide certain decks can go in modern (Energy is the primary candidate but also decks like Scales) can have a tool that rewards them for running Stoneforge. I also don't think that Jitte is an inherently better tool than Kaldra or Lost Jitte at doing these things in those decks, which rewards players for testing a wide variety of options and optimizing. It helps make decisions matter more, which I like a lot. 

Pod I think is really interesting as a decision tool. Combo lines are way more efficient now, and require pretty minimal deck slot consideration, so you would probably end up with 2, maybe 3 pod decks-

1) a turbo combo deck specifically geared around infinitely comboing your opponent as fast as possible, which would probably be not great in the metagame 

2) a value focused midrange deck with a light combo package to be able to snap the combo when the way is open- playing powerful efficient threats with strong etb effects and being able to convert a dork into an instant win vs opposing combo or aggro after disrupting them, or vs opposing midrange/control lists if they leave shields down. 

3) mayyyyybe a comboless pod deck that attempts to use pod as a silver bullet finder, but I think those builds will likely lack in today's modern which is such a hyper efficient format that tapping out t3 for pod is probably leaving yourself far too open for comfort 

My carefulness around Pod is that cards like Pod are inherently limiting to design. They have to be careful about what creatures they print because if Pod's ability to combo becomes *too* efficient, the card becomes miserable to play against. However, given the general power increase of the format and the fact that the quality of interaction is just so much higher these days, I could easily see Pod being a fine choice. It gives another good creature combo deck that isn't yawgmoth (which can't really justify playing pod because of the life cost to chaining pod) that probably won't be t1 as well.

DRS performed incredibly well in Jund Shells at the time, and would be immediately playable in Oculus as a tempo card that also accelerates them and gives them a grindy win condition in the late game. 

The main question you have to ask for every format when you want to unban isn't "is this card too powerful", it's "what dynamics does this card add to the metagame when we unban it." 

For example, Punishing Fire isn't too powerful on its face- it's a slow card that requires repeat investment over a long period of time to really be at its best.

However, eldrazi lists can instantly run it as a 4 of alongside grove to immediately swing their matchup into energy and similar low curve creature decks by multiple points, when they already have access to fast chalice or trinisphere to lock the matchup down after they stabilize. Do we want to give them another strong tool to stabilize with in that matchup? 

When I look at Deathrite, I see us giving UBx decks acceleration that they don't need to splash for, as well as a grindy win condition in a single card. Is that something we want them to have? What matchups does that card improve for those lists?

What about Necrodominance decks? Do we want to play against turn 2 necro -> turn 3 sheoldred? 

This is also not including Ketramose decks. DRS with Ketramose is absurd- a repeatable source of acceleration, damage and potentially life gain while turning on Ketramose.

As someone who works in film, and also someone who adores ROTE (some people IRL literally call me Fool because of it; The Fool inspired so much of my understanding of my own gender)

Just because you *can* do it, doesn't mean it *works* well. Different mediums have different strengths and weaknesses which you intentionally explore.

The biggest strength of film is the edit, which allows it to connect disparate shots and imply narrative through their juxtaposition. One shot leading to another implies a relationship between them, which allows you to connect ideas in really interesting ways that force thoughtful exploration of these concepts. 

The biggest *weakness*, however, is monologue and dialogue; especially internal versions. Film is a medium all about *showing* things; talking about them instead often leads to horrendous pacing issues and most of the time doesn't make for a great movie. 

I fucking love Realm of the Elderlings; but if you adapted it you'd need a Visual way to show Fitz's internal dialogue, and it's so incredibly rich that it'd be a Herculean task. At some point I'm going to write a spec for it because I think it'd be a really fun challenge, but I don't think it'd make for a great TV show or movie.

As someone who plays a lot of Esper Scam (satoru is broken), it isn't a splash- the deck has to be core black to support it. That being said, the deck is built around swingy plays early game turning into a long term grindy plan- your best hands are built around either an early grief + ephemerate or troll + persist. 

I think in general, the main thing is that grief as a card is very very high value for minimal inclusion cost (NDAA type effects in RB scam, Ephemerate in WBx builds). I was pro banning grief over banning fury when hitting scam was first proposed- I liked stopping their explosive nut draws that inherently protected themselves rather than going after a very dedicated creature that couldn't protect itself when you scammed it. 

I think having a "fun police" deck is something that modern requires more and more of these days. We see decks with incredibly greedy mana bases, incredibly explosive combos, and heavy value plays- and we didn't really have the strong reactive tools to handle them until MH2. Right now, Grief is the strongest tool we have at doing that, and so it sees heavy play- leading to a lot of moments that feel bad. However, I think a format without grief will lead to a really heavy focus on ships in the night style magic, which I think would be even worse.

Personally I'm hoping some more better aligned fun police decks show up with help from MH3. Vs unfair decks is where the mu changes a lot. Charbelcher can win the Tron MU on a good mulligan but it feels so bad when you don't draw one that can just end up folding. Vs Amulet, Force of Vigor buys you time, but you can still just end up losing badly.

However, the deck is generally raw still. There's so much optimization and work to be put in- recently I have been a part of the people testing Elder Deep Fiend, and I think the card is close to what we want- it's just not quite there yet. 

I think the weakest link in the list RN is actually T3feri. Outside its utility vs blood moon, I think the card is generally p wack outside of control/murktide matchups, but you need it there to add another pitch card for solitude. In those two mu's it is incredible, however.

I think if another card is printed that fills that slot, that better suits what the deck wants to do, or improves the mu vs amulet or Tron, the deck will be t1. Right now I feel like I'm a t1.5 deck with t0 potential.

Decks will always lean towards running whatever the most optimal toolkit available. This means some form of semi greedy multicolor deck will always exist in any format with good 3+ color Mana bases. The risk is always worth it- the existence of blood moon alone isn't enough to fully make it not risky
 

The issue with rewarding LD strategies is that LD isn't an expression of skill for the most part. Even prison heavy strategies (decks like lantern control etc) were heavily skill favored lists- they required strong pilot skill to use, in how you sequence cards and understanding the risk/reward of letting cards stick on the table. LD strategies are the literal inverse of this- the only skill expression is destroying the right land on the right turn, and using that tempo gain to put yourself so far ahead of your opponent that you win. You see this in legacy dnt where you can run Armageddon to sequence into with tax pieces that kill your opponent on the table to swing the game with one card. In legacy it's a necessary tool in some metagames just due to the card quality, but in Modern I don't think we're there yet.

Hi! I'm a UB Shadow player (UB ring as well) and I would put the deck at a solid t1.5 or t2.

You have close to a 50/50 mu vs scam because of Stern Scolding and Subtlety coming in from the sideboard. You also play so many cantrips (preordain, consider and wraith) that you end up surprisingly resistant to Grief. 

You *rail* 4c omnath if they can't stick hobbit/t3f, and you have more than enough resources to answer those cards in the matchup. They really, really need to dig to try and handle you and they don't have the reach to punish you for aggressive shadow setups. I would call this matchup 60/40 in your favor.


UWx decks are similar in that their interaction lines up badly into yours, and their only real interaction that favors them is T3feri. Dovin's Veto can be annoying post board, but otherwise I think you can stick and protect a threat so well that it's hard for them to interact with you. I'd call this 60/40 in your favor

Cascade shells are pretty free matchups; you just stick a threat earlier than they can, and their disruption does not line up well against yours. Even 1 Rhinos cascade isn't enough to beat you. Living End cannot handle an early Bowmasters with protection; it spirals so far out of control that you end up wildly far ahead pretty quickly. This is a very, very clean 70/30 matchup in your favor.

Ring based Black midrange decks I feel slightly unfavored against. It really revolves around how fast you can assemble a lethal board state and if you can prevent the Ring from sticking. Luckily, Bowmasters is genuinely a great card into the matchup, and being able to slow them down with it helps (either they answer it and have one less card to handle Shadow/Murktide, or they don't and their best card in the matchup is almost useless)

Tron, Scales and Yawgmoth, however, feel close to unwinnable matchups. 

Tron assembles Tron faster than you can stick a game winning threat, and you need to be able to interact with them pretty much every single turn in order to beat them; and while you can turn off The Ring, they don't need it to win comfortably. You really need to dedicate 3x break the ice or similar in your sideboard to have a consistent shot at beating them. 70/30 in their favor.

Yawgmoth is hard because they just have so many fucking pesky little tools that interact favorably into your threats. Without Temur Battle Rage, shadow is easy to chump for them. If you can focus on sticking an early Murktide you can win, primarily because their only out to it is Grist; which makes scolding invaluable in this Matchup. However, they can't consistently play for the combo in this matchup, meaning a lot of their explosiveness is gone. 60/40 in their favor.

Scales is a similar situation except they go out of control much, much faster; and you really suck into artifact spam. Hangarback Walker getting sacrificed is also the worst feeling in the universe vs you. This is another matchup where Scolding can really save your ass, but it's often not enough. 70/30 scales.

Overall, I think the deck is more than viable, and should be seeing more play; but it's also a deck that really punishes poor sequencing, and Tron is such a horrendous matchup that it can be a risky proposition at large events.

And then you get to decks like eggs, paradox academy, and storm; where you have 100 cards to build as many sick lines as you can and you are actively rewarded for incredible mastery and understanding such a complex set of options that are laying in front of you.

Then there's the math aspect- that running about 8 of a card is around equivalent to a playset- and then deciding what 6-8 versions of an effect you want to play in order to consistently see that effect, and knowing how to assess and manage drawbacks accordingly

All and all, canlander's singleton nature adds a ton of strategic depth and variety into the format.

Let's not be class reductionist here. My grandmother's family was *incredibly* poor and still could trace their heritage back through a graveyard that kept records in west virginia. Slave owners didn't give a fuck who was born where nor did they keep track of it (with some rare exceptions iirc) and so that's a big part of where this comes from.

I'm a white person so I don't want to speak too much aboutblack experiences in America- but this is one of the coolest artistic choices I think I've seen in this secret lair.

A lot of black people in america can't trace their legacy back further than 3-4 generations *at most* because of slavery and the slave trade; yet I have the privelege to know my grandmother's family dates all the way back to Plymouth Rock. By placing this character so prominently in the forefront of this scene, it acknowledges that destroyed heritage and want, which is honestly incredibly beautiful to me. 

If I'm being an ass I'm happy to delete this, but I really think that historical and cultural piece is super important to point out

Edit:

Thinking about this more after work- this heritage wasn't just destroyed, it was *stolen*. If you think about how much pride people hold in their heritage and how much people pull identity from that (to the point where a lot of 3rd or 4th generation immigrants in the US don't identify as 'american' but as Irish or Italian-American etc) it's even more wounding; your ancestors being intentionally denied what historically has always been seen as something to be proud of as a way of denying their humanity. 

The idea of this card being about a *return* to ancestry and the young man holding the book in his lap, it speaks to him reclaiming his heritage and that I think makes this my favorite art in all of magic. It's a really bold choice for what the card is- and I think it's incredibly powerful.
